t: Number of Distinct Binary Strings After Applying Operations
o: Flipping any length-k substring any number of times generates a set of reachable strings; count them mod 1e9+7. Key observation: flips commute and are self-inverse, so reachable strings correspond to subsets of the n−k+1 flip positions — but two different subsets can give the same string only if their XOR is a combination of flips producing the all-zero change, which never happens unless the subsets are equal (each flip position affects a unique window pattern; the (n−k+1) window vectors are linearly independent because each has a leading 1 at its own start). Hence the count is exactly 2^(n−k+1). Example 1: n=4, k=3 → 2^2 = 4 ✓. Example 2: 2^1 = 2 ✓.
k: Flip operations form a vector space over GF(2); the n−k+1 window-flip vectors are linearly independent.
Therefore every subset of operations yields a distinct string: answer = 2^(n−k+1) mod 1e9+7.
Fast exponentiation handles n up to 1e5 instantly.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Enumeration (small inputs only)
a.i: BFS/DFS over all flip-position subsets, collecting resulting strings in a set. Exponential — only to verify the pattern on tiny examples.
s: Start from s; enumerate all 2^(n−k+1) subsets of window starts.
XOR-apply chosen windows to get each string; insert into a set.
Return set size (conceptually; infeasible beyond n−k+1 ≈ 20).
a.t: O(2^m · n · k), m = n−k+1 — exponential, illustrative only

a.n: Approach 2: Linear Algebra Insight + Fast Power (Optimal)
a.i: Each window-start flip is an independent basis vector over GF(2) (window i is the only one flipping position i without flipping earlier positions in a triangular argument), so all 2^(n−k+1) operation subsets give distinct results.
s: Return pow(2, m, 1e9+7) via fast exponentiation.

w: Lead with the independence argument: order windows left to right; window i is the only one affecting position i once earlier windows are fixed, proving injectivity of subset → string. Pitfall: trying to simulate for large n. Follow-up: what if flips were of varying lengths, or applied to substrings of size exactly k chosen adaptively?
